summaries.example: Imagine a school choosing a playground rule. A rule may be accepted because students trust the principal, because it has always been used, or because students had a fair chance to discuss and approve it. Philosophers ask whether acceptance alone makes the rule legitimate, or whether the rule and the way it was made must also be justified.
summaries.summary: Political legitimacy asks when political power and political decisions are acceptable or justified. One approach describes legitimacy as people’s belief that a government has the right to rule. Another asks whether that belief is supported by good reasons. Philosophers distinguish an authority that merely gets people to obey from an authority that truly has a right to rule. They also ask whether legitimacy mainly justifies coercion, such as enforcing laws, or mainly justifies authority itself. Some theories say legitimate authority creates political obligations, while others separate the right to rule from a duty to obey. The entry compares possible sources of legitimacy, including consent, public reasoning, participation, good results, and special knowledge. It also examines whether democracy is required, whether fair procedures are enough, and whether the quality of decisions matters too. Finally, it asks how legitimacy applies beyond individual countries to international and global institutions.
key_ideas: Legitimacy can describe what people believe about a government, or it can ask whether that government is really justified.
A government may be effective at making people obey without having a genuine right to rule.
Some philosophers connect legitimacy mainly to justified force; others connect it to justified authority.
Legitimate authority may create a duty to obey, but some philosophers say extra conditions are needed.
Disagreement exists about whether fair procedures, good results, or both make decisions legitimate.
Questions about legitimacy can apply to states and also to international or global institutions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Governments make rules that affect everyone, sometimes using penalties to enforce them. Thinking about legitimacy helps us ask whether this power is being used in a way that people can reasonably accept, whether people are treated as equals, and whether those making decisions are answerable to those affected.

important_terms.definition: A quality that makes a government, law, or decision acceptable or justified to the people affected by it.
The recognized right to give rules or commands. A group can have power without having this right.
Using pressure or force to make people do something, such as enforcing a law with penalties.
A duty people may have to follow political rules or commands. Philosophers disagree about when this duty exists.

questions_to_think_about: Is a rule legitimate just because most people accept it?
Can a government be fair in its decision-making but still make an unjust decision?
When, if ever, should people have a duty to obey a government?
Should people affected by an international rule have a voice in making it?

summaries.example: Suppose a government passes an emergency law after a public debate and a vote. One view asks whether the law was produced through an inclusive and fair procedure. Another asks whether the law protects freedom and equality or produces sufficiently good results. A third asks whether the government was justified in using penalties to enforce it at all. These questions can yield different judgments: a decision might be legitimate without being fully just, because legitimacy can make weaker demands than justice.
summaries.summary:
Political legitimacy is studied in both descriptive and normative ways. Descriptively, it concerns beliefs that a political order or authority is rightful; these beliefs can help explain stable patterns of obedience. Normatively, it concerns whether political power, authority, and perhaps political obligations are justified. The entry distinguishes effective or de facto authority from legitimate authority. It also distinguishes legitimacy from justice: on influential views, legitimacy is a weaker requirement, so an institution can be legitimate yet unjust, though the precise relationship depends on the theory. A major debate asks whether legitimacy is fundamentally about justifying coercion or about justifying a right to rule. Another asks whether legitimate authority necessarily produces a duty to obey, since some philosophers separate authority from political obligation.

The entry surveys several sources of legitimacy. Consent theories emphasize actual, tacit, hypothetical, or normative agreement. Public-reason theories ask whether coercion can be justified by reasons that reasonable citizens can share. Participation theories emphasize equal political influence. Fact-based and epistemic theories instead appeal to good consequences, normative standards, or the capacity to reach correct decisions. In debates about democracy, instrumentalists value democracy for its outcomes, pure proceduralists value the fairness or equality of the process, and mixed theories combine procedural and substantive standards. Finally, political cosmopolitanism extends the legitimacy problem beyond states to international and global institutions, raising questions about accountability, coercion, justice, consent, and democracy at a global level.
key_ideas: The descriptive and normative concepts of legitimacy should not be simply identified. A regime may be widely accepted yet still be unjustified, while normative legitimacy asks for a standard of justification.

A central dispute concerns whether legitimacy primarily justifies political authority or the state’s coercive power. Authority concerns a right to rule; coercion concerns restrictions backed by force or threats.
Legitimate authority and political obligation may come apart. Some accounts say authority generates a duty to obey; others require consent, membership, or further moral conditions.
Legitimacy is not identical to justice on every theory. A political institution may satisfy a weaker standard of legitimacy while still failing to realize full justice.
The sources of legitimacy include actual or hypothetical consent, public justification, equal participation, beneficial consequences, conformity with normative facts, and epistemic advantages.
Democratic theories divide between outcome-focused instrumentalism, procedure-focused views, and mixed views that assess both decision procedures and results.
summaries.why_it_matters: Political institutions claim authority over people who may disagree with their laws and decisions. Legitimacy provides a framework for evaluating that claim without assuming that effectiveness, majority support, justice, or democracy automatically settles the matter. It also helps explain why global organizations face legitimacy problems when they make rules or attach consequences beyond national borders.

important_terms.definition: A normative property of political institutions or decisions: being justified or acceptable, especially when political power or coercion is exercised.
A descriptive idea concerning people’s beliefs or acceptance that an institution or ruler has the right to govern.
A claimed or actual right to rule and issue commands, possibly backed by enforcement.
The use of threats, penalties, or force to restrict people’s choices or secure compliance.
The moral or political requirement to obey a state or political authority; its connection to legitimacy is disputed.
Reasons or standards that citizens can share despite disagreement about deeper moral or religious doctrines.
The view that legitimacy depends only on features of a decision-making process, such as fair participation, rather than on the decision’s result.
The view that political legitimacy is not limited to nation-states and may concern international or global institutions.

questions_to_think_about: What is lost if legitimacy means only popular acceptance? What is lost if it means only moral justification?
Does a fair democratic procedure legitimate an outcome that is substantively unjust?
Can legitimate authority exist without generating a general duty to obey?
Should political decision-makers defer to experts when experts are more likely to be correct?
What standards should apply to global institutions that make rules affecting people across borders?

summaries.example: A town council wants to limit cars near a school. Some residents say the rule is legitimate if elected representatives followed fair procedures and everyone had a chance to speak. Others say that is not enough: the rule must also protect children without unfairly burdening some families. A different view asks whether the council has the right to enforce the rule with fines. The example shows why legitimacy can involve the process, the result, and the use of force.
summaries.summary:
Political legitimacy concerns when political institutions and their decisions deserve acceptance or have a justified claim to rule. The entry begins with a descriptive idea: a regime may be called legitimate because people believe in its authority or accept its commands. A normative idea asks a different question: is the institution or decision actually justified? This difference matters because a government can be stable and effective while still lacking a justified right to rule.

The entry then examines the function of legitimacy. One family of theories connects it to political authority, understood as a right to issue commands. Another connects it to coercion, asking when a state may rightfully restrict people’s choices or punish them for disobedience. Many theories link legitimacy with political obligations, but some philosophers argue that having a legitimate authority does not by itself give everyone a general duty to obey. The entry also separates legitimacy from justice in several theories: legitimacy can be a lower threshold than full justice.

Philosophers propose different sources of legitimacy. Consent theories emphasize agreement; public-reason theories emphasize reasons citizens can share; participation theories emphasize equal influence; and other theories focus on good results or political knowledge. These disagreements continue in theories of democracy. Some judge democracy by its results, some by fair procedures, and some by both. The discussion also extends to international and global institutions, where questions of coercion, accountability, consent, and democratic participation arise beyond the nation-state.
key_ideas: A government can be successful at making people obey without being legitimate. Effectiveness and a right to rule are different ideas.
Some philosophers think legitimacy is mainly about whether coercive power is justified; others think it is mainly about whether political authority is justified.
Consent is one proposed source of legitimacy, but philosophers debate whether consent must be real, clearly expressed, or only hypothetical.
Other theories emphasize public reasoning, equal participation, good consequences, or the ability to make knowledgeable decisions.
Democracy may be defended because it produces better results, because it treats citizens as political equals, or because fair procedures themselves matter.
Legitimacy and justice are related but are not always the same. A legitimate institution might still fall short of complete justice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Laws and political decisions shape people’s freedom, opportunities, and responsibilities. Legitimacy helps us evaluate whether those decisions are made by institutions with a justified claim to govern. It encourages careful distinctions: being popular is not automatically being justified, being just is not always the same as being legitimate, and having authority may not automatically settle whether obedience is required.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a government, institution, or decision has a justified right to rule or be accepted.
A right to make rules or commands for others, not merely the ability to make them obey.
Pressure, threats, or force used by political institutions to secure obedience to rules.
An obligation to follow political commands or laws. Philosophers disagree about whether legitimate authority always creates one.
The view of legitimacy based on what people believe or accept, rather than on an independent standard of justification.
The view that legitimacy depends on whether political power or decisions meet a standard of justification or acceptability.
A democratic ideal in which public decisions are supported by reasons that citizens can share despite deeper disagreements.
The position that democratic legitimacy depends mainly or entirely on fair decision-making procedures.

questions_to_think_about: Can people’s belief in a government make it legitimate, or must there be other reasons?
Is a fair vote enough to make a decision legitimate?
Why might someone support a duty to obey only when extra conditions are met?
Would a government with expert leaders be legitimate if it made better decisions but gave citizens less political control?
How should legitimacy work for institutions that govern across countries?
